scale_010:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (but not finalize) the setup of our {{vendor}} data warehouse for the 'Data warehouse & BI' initiative. This step requires explicit human sign-off before any billing commitment or root credential creation, so your job is to research and draft everything needed for my review — not to provision anything.

If missing, ask me for: my expected monthly data volume and query workload, the preferred cloud region(s) for data residency, the teams/roles that will need access, and my rough budget ceiling.

Please do the following:
1. Research {{vendor}}'s current pricing model (compute credits, storage, any free tier or trial with real query capability, no credit card required) and produce a written estimate of monthly cost based on my stated workload.
2. Summarize how {{vendor}} supports region/residency selection for data storage, and confirm which regions fit my requirement.
3. Draft a role-based access control plan: proposed roles, table/column/row-level restrictions, and any masking policies needed so multiple teams can share one warehouse safely.
4. Draft recommended budget guardrails: auto-suspend settings, resource monitors, or spend alerts to prevent runaway queries or idle compute costs.
5. Compile all of this into a single setup checklist/document, including the account creation form fields pre-filled where possible (organization name, region, initial admin role, budget monitor thresholds).

Done looks like: a complete, reviewable document containing the cost estimate, region choice, access-control plan, budget guardrail settings, and a pre-filled setup checklist — with no account created, no billing enabled, and no credentials generated.

Report back with the full document plus a short summary of key decisions needing my input (region, budget cap, roles). Since provisioning commits us to billing and creates root data-access credentials, you must stop for human sign-off before creating the warehouse, enabling billing, or generating any credentials.

scale_010:n2.prompt:
You are helping me configure {{vendor}} (customer data platform) sources as part of setting up our data warehouse & BI pipeline. Before starting, ask me for: (1) our {{vendor}} account/workspace details or confirm you can reach it via my configured credentials, (2) the list of production systems/apps we want to instrument (web app, mobile app, backend services, and any third-party cloud apps like support or billing tools we want data pulled from), and (3) our target warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery) so downstream routing lines up later.

Then, using {{vendor}}'s documented API or MCP server (never direct HTTP calls):
1. Draft a proposed source configuration for each system: name, type (web/mobile SDK, server-to-server HTTP ingestion, or third-party cloud app connector), and the events/objects it should send (track, identify, page calls as relevant).
2. For server-side sources, prepare the server-to-server ingestion setup including authentication method (referencing my configured credentials only, never exposing secrets) and delivery guarantee settings.
3. For third-party cloud app data, identify the appropriate pull-based connector and draft its configuration (auth scope, sync frequency).
4. Compile a single change plan document listing every source to be created, its type, and expected event volume/frequency, plus any destination wiring needed downstream.

Do not create, activate, or wire any sources yet — this requires a human explicitly approves before changes are applied. Present the full draft configuration and change plan, then stop for human sign-off.

Report back with: the list of proposed sources and their configs, any open questions (e.g., missing credentials, ambiguous event naming), and a clear note that you are awaiting my approval before applying anything in {{vendor}}.

scale_010:n3.prompt:
You are helping me draft data warehouse data models as part of setting up our Data warehouse & BI stack (Snowflake or BigQuery feeding Metabase dashboards). Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) which warehouse we use (Snowflake or BigQuery), (b) a list of our production source systems/databases and their key tables (e.g. users, orders, subscriptions, events), and (c) the business questions or dashboards we want Metabase to answer (e.g. revenue trends, churn, funnel conversion).

2. Based on my answers, draft a proposed data model: a set of staging tables (one per source table, lightly cleaned), and downstream fact and dimension tables (e.g. fact_orders, dim_customers, dim_products) sized for our reporting needs. For each table, list the proposed columns, data types, primary/foreign keys, and the source table(s) it derives from.

3. Write this out as a clear schema document (markdown or SQL DDL comments) including: table names, column definitions, grain of each fact table, and any obvious derived/calculated fields (e.g. order total, days since signup).

4. Note any assumptions you made about naming conventions, schema/dataset organization, and partitioning or clustering keys, and flag any source data gaps you noticed.

5. Do not create or apply any tables, schemas, or DDL in the actual warehouse — only prepare the draft model document for review.

When done, report back with the full draft schema document, a short summary of the fact/dimension tables proposed, and the list of open questions or assumptions. Then stop for human sign-off before any changes are applied to the warehouse.

scale_010:n4.prompt:
You are helping me configure {{vendor}} (our customer data platform) to sync event data into our Snowflake data warehouse. This step requires human approval before changes are applied — you must prepare everything but not execute the final activation.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available in configured credentials or environment context: our {{vendor}} workspace details, our Snowflake account identifier, target database/schema name, and the list of event sources already flowing into {{vendor}} (e.g., production app, backend services).

Then do the following:
1. Using {{vendor}}'s documented API (or MCP server if available) and configured credentials, inspect existing sources connected to our {{vendor}} workspace and confirm which ones should route to Snowflake.
2. Draft the configuration for a new Snowflake destination in {{vendor}}: connection parameters (account, warehouse, database, schema), sync schedule/frequency, and which event streams/sources should be mapped to it, including any per-destination filtering or field mapping you recommend.
3. Check whether {{vendor}} requires a Snowflake user/role with specific grants for loading data, and draft the SQL or setup steps needed to create that role, without executing them.
4. Prepare a clear summary document listing: sources to be routed, destination config, sync schedule, and any warehouse-side setup required.
5. Do not activate the destination, do not run any warehouse grant statements, and do not enable the sync — stop for human sign-off once your prepared plan and drafts are ready.

Report back with: the sources identified, the full draft destination configuration, any warehouse setup SQL/steps you drafted, open questions or risks (e.g., schema conflicts, cost implications of sync frequency), and a checklist of exactly what remains for me to review and approve before you proceed.

scale_010:n5.prompt:
You are helping me verify that the data pipelines feeding our data warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery, whichever we use) are running correctly and that Metabase dashboards reflect fresh data. This is an async check: pipeline runs complete on their own schedule, so you must poll/monitor rather than expect instant results.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available in our configured tools: the data warehouse platform in use, the names/IDs of the pipeline jobs or ETL tool (e.g. Fivetran, Airbyte, custom scripts) moving data from production systems, and the Metabase dashboard URLs or workspace to check.

Then do the following:
1. Check the pipeline/orchestration tool's run history or logs for the most recent scheduled or triggered runs — confirm each completed successfully, note timestamps, and flag any failures, partial loads, or stale runs (no run in the expected window).
2. Query the warehouse (via its console or configured connector) to confirm row counts or last-updated timestamps in key tables look current and reasonable compared to production source volumes.
3. Open the relevant Metabase dashboards and confirm the underlying data reflects the latest warehouse refresh (check 'last synced' or data freshness indicators if visible).
4. If a pipeline run is still in progress or scheduled for later, note that and plan to re-check after the expected completion window — do not treat this as a failure yet.

Report back with: a status table listing each pipeline, its last successful run time, row/data freshness check result, and Metabase dashboard freshness confirmation. Clearly flag any broken, stalled, or delayed pipelines needing my attention, and note which items are still pending and will need a follow-up poll.

scale_010:n6.prompt:
You are helping me set up Metabase dashboards connected to our data warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery) as part of our data warehouse & BI pipeline. Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already provided: our Metabase instance URL (self-hosted or Metabase Cloud), the warehouse type and connection details (host, database/project, warehouse/dataset, schema), which schemas or tables should be exposed to Metabase, and the business questions or KPIs we want dashboards to answer (e.g. revenue, signups, churn, pipeline health).

Using your configured credentials, connect to Metabase and prepare (but do not finalize) the following: (1) a draft data source connection configuration pointing to our warehouse, (2) a set of proposed 'questions' (SQL or GUI-built queries) covering the KPIs I specified, (3) draft dashboards grouping related questions with sensible layout and filters, and (4) a summary of any permissions/collections structure needed for team access. Document every proposed change clearly - connection settings, query logic, dashboard structure - so I can review it in full before anything is applied to the live Metabase instance.

Do not create the actual data source connection, publish dashboards, or grant permissions in Metabase yet. Once your draft plan and configurations are ready, present them to me as a clear checklist with all proposed settings, queries, and dashboard layouts, and then stop for human sign-off before any changes are applied. After I approve, wait for my explicit confirmation before proceeding to implement anything in the live system.

scale_010:n7.prompt:
You are helping me prepare an executive dashboard in Metabase, connected to our data warehouse (Snowflake or BigQuery). Please do the following, asking me for any missing details before proceeding:

1. Ask me for: (a) which warehouse we use and how Metabase is connected to it, (b) the business areas leadership cares about (e.g. revenue, growth, churn, cash, pipeline), and (c) any existing tables/views already built for reporting.
2. Propose a draft list of 8-12 candidate KPIs grouped by business area (e.g. MRR, new customers, churn rate, CAC, runway, active users), with a one-line definition and the source table/field for each, based on what's available in the warehouse.
3. For each candidate KPI, draft the underlying Metabase query (using Metabase's query builder or SQL editor) and specify the recommended chart type (line, bar, number, funnel, etc.) and suggested time grain (daily/weekly/monthly).
4. Design a proposed dashboard layout: which metrics go at the top as headline numbers, which are trend charts, and how they're grouped/sectioned.
5. Compile all of this into a single written proposal: KPI list with definitions and sources, draft queries, chart types, and layout mockup description, plus a short explanation of any tradeoffs or assumptions made in selecting the KPIs.
6. Do NOT create or publish the dashboard in Metabase yet, and do not finalize which KPIs represent company priorities — that decision belongs to leadership.

Report back with the complete proposal (KPI list, queries, chart types, layout) so the executive can review and choose which metrics to include, reorder priorities, or request changes. Clearly state that this is a draft and stop for human sign-off before building or publishing anything in Metabase.
